title: NASA 'troubleshooting' transporter for space station's robotic arm [Updated]
gist: After a routine walk-off maneuver, the ISS's mobile transporter that carries Canadarm2 showed communication errors; NASA says the arm itself works and expects to resolve the issue before Crew-13. The episode highlights the aging ISS and the arm's importance for berthing Cygnus and HTV-X cargo craft as SpaceX plans to retire Dragon within four years.

insights.claim: After a routine walk-off maneuver, engineers noted operational issues with the ISS's Canadarm2 robotic arm and the mobile transporter that guides it along the station's truss.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Hardware faults on aging ISS infrastructure could disrupt station operations and contractor schedules.

insights.claim: NASA says Canadarm2 is operating as expected but non-robotic mobile transporter components showed communication errors, and NASA and SpaceX are checking for GPS interference with Dragon docking, expecting resolution before Crew-13.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Near-term crew rotation appears on track, limiting schedule risk for SpaceX.
insights.quote: Joint teams are actively conducting the analysis and expect to resolve the issue before the Crew-13 launch.

insights.claim: Canadarm2, built by MDA and launched in April 2001, had a 15-year design lifetime and has been operating more than a decade beyond it.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Over-age hardware raises failure risk across the ISS.
insights.quote: Its nominal design lifetime was 15 years, so it has been operating for more than a decade beyond this point.

insights.claim: Losing the arm's berthing capability could seriously affect cargo missions, because NASA's other main cargo vehicles, Northrop's Cygnus and Japan's HTV-X, cannot dock autonomously and SpaceX plans to retire Dragon within four years.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: ISS resupply depends on a single aging arm, a concentration risk for NASA and its cargo contractors.
insights.locator: Can an armless space station survive?

insights.claim: The arm also moves large hardware like cooling pumps for spacewalks; NASA could probably work around its loss, but operations would become more difficult.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Degraded capability would raise ISS operating costs and complexity.
insights.locator: The robotic arm is also used

insights.claim: With the ISS nearing its 30th anniversary, the author warns its so-far graceful aging may not continue, while NASA's contracting for private replacement stations has not gone smoothly.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A gap between ISS decline and commercial station readiness is a key risk for the commercial LEO sector.
insights.quote: So far, most of the aging process has been graceful, but that does not necessarily mean this run of good fortune (and preparation) will continue.
insights.locator: The potential loss of the robotic arm
